lesson.title: From Message to Molecule: How Translation Builds a Protein
lesson.summary: Translation is the process by which a ribosome reads mRNA codons and uses matching tRNAs to link amino acids together into a protein, proceeding through initiation, elongation, and termination.
lesson.body:
Translation is where everything covered so far in this unit comes together. A processed mRNA, carrying its cap, its tail, and its correctly spliced sequence of exons, meets a ribosome in the cytoplasm, either a free ribosome or one bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, and the two work together to convert a message written in nucleotides into a protein written in amino acids.

Translation begins with initiation. A small ribosomal subunit, together with an initiator tRNA carrying methionine, associates with the mRNA and, in eukaryotic cells, generally starts near the 5' cap before moving along the message until it locates the AUG start codon. Once that start codon is found, the large ribosomal subunit joins the complex, forming a complete ribosome with the initiator tRNA sitting in what is called the P site, ready to begin building a protein.

From there, translation moves into elongation, which repeats over and over as the protein grows. An incoming charged tRNA, carrying an amino acid attached by its matching aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, enters the ribosome's A site only if its anticodon correctly pairs with the next codon on the mRNA. The ribosome then catalyzes formation of a peptide bond between the amino acid held by the tRNA in the P site and the amino acid held by the new tRNA in the A site, a reaction carried out largely by the ribosomal RNA of the large subunit itself, meaning the ribosome is acting as a ribozyme, an RNA that catalyzes a chemical reaction. After the bond forms, the ribosome shifts one codon further along the mRNA, moving the tRNAs from the A site to the P site and from the P site onward to an exit, or E, site, which frees the A site to accept the next matching tRNA. This cycle repeats codon by codon, with the mRNA read 5' to 3' and the growing polypeptide chain extended from its N-terminus toward its C-terminus.

Elongation continues until a stop codon, UAA, UAG, or UGA, enters the A site. Because no tRNA pairs with a stop codon, a release factor binds there instead, prompting the finished polypeptide to be released from the last tRNA and the ribosomal subunits to separate from the mRNA and from each other, freeing them to be recycled for another round of translation. Because a ribosome clears the region around the start codon fairly early in this process, another ribosome can often begin its own round of initiation on the very same mRNA before the first one has finished, which is exactly how multiple ribosomes end up translating one message at the same time.
